Section I: Introduction and Overview
Overview of Activist Hedge Funds
• Activist hedge funds acquire significant stakes in public companies where they believe shareholder value is constrained by governance or strategic inefficiencies
• The goal is to unlock value by actively influencing management decisions
• Returns depend on the successful execution of the activist campaign rather than passive participation in equity markets

Section I: Introduction and Overview
Why Activist Hedge Funds Work
The Agency Problem
Consequences
• Capital misallocation: Investment decisions prioritize risk avoidance over return on invested capital
• Managers are expected to maximize shareholder value, but their personal incentives often differ from those of shareholders -> conflict of interest
• Excess cash retention: Cash is held on the balance sheet or deployed into low-return uses instead of being distributed to shareholders
• Management may prioritize compensation, job security or reputation over long-term value creation
• Fragmented ownership and insufficient board oversight limit effective monitoring and accountability of management decisions
• Delayed portfolio optimization: Underperforming assets or business units are kept for too long due to resistance to divestment or restructuring
• Rising operating inefficiency: Weakened accountability leads to increased operating costs and structural complexity

Key takeaway: Management does not always act in the way that maximizes shareholder value due to limited accountability and misaligned personal incentives. Activist hedge funds address this agency problem by increasing oversight and pressure on management to encourage decisions that are better aligned with shareholder interests and long-
term value creation.

Section II: Different Types of Activist Hedge Funds
Structural Activism
Definition
Main players
• Objective: Addressing the conglomerate discount of an organization where the market fails to value a company’s individual business units in their current bundling
• Founder: Paul Singer • Founded: 1977 • Strategy: Value gap analysis, push for divestment • Annual Returns: 14.2% (2023) • AUM: $73bn (2025)
• Tactics: Aggressive push for spin-off or carve-out of non-core assets, optimizing the capital structure through debt recapitalization, and facilitating divestures or take-private transactions
• Founder: Chris Hohn • Founded: 2003 • Strategy: Value gap analysis, push for divestment • Annual Returns: 27.8% (2025) • AUM: $77bn (2025)
Structural activism often relies on a sum-of-the-parts valuation, where business units are valued separately using industry multiples.
The gap between implied standalone value and market valuation represents the conglomerate discount the activist aims to unlock.

Section IV: Limitations & Risk

Section IV: Limitations & Risk
Why Activism Is High-Conviction and High-Risk
Time Horizon & Capital Lock-Up
Why Activism Is High-Conviction

• Activist campaigns typically require 12–36 months to play out • Capital is effectively locked while outcomes depend on board response and shareholder votes • Limited liquidity compared with traditional long-only equity strategies

• Clear agency problem: Dispersed ownership and weak monitoring create opportunities for value-enhancing intervention • Identifiable, actionable catalysts: Board changes, capital allocation shifts, asset sales, or strategic alternatives • Empirical support: Activist engagement is associated with positive abnormal returns on average, despite wide dispersion
Why Risk Is Structurally Elevated

• Minority ownership model: Activists intentionally operate without control • Binary, path-dependent outcomes: Success depends on execution, not valuation alone • External dependencies: Outcomes influenced by markets, regulation, and third-party voters
Extended timelines convert valuation risk into execution and governance risk

Section IV: Limitations & Risk
Market & Capital Market Risk
Market Environment Matters
Litigation

• Robust M&A activity, elevated equity volatility, and constructive financing conditions supported a record 255 activist campaigns globally • Market conditions materially influence both the feasibility and timing of activist exits
Activist Theses Are Increasingly M&A-Dependent
Poison Pills

• Exit feasibility is market-dependent: widening credit spreads reduce buyer financing capacity and transaction certainty • Private equity bids weaken as leverage becomes more expensive, reducing strategic alternatives • Regulatory intervention can delay or block transactions, extending holding periods • Sector concentration amplifies risk: activist campaigns cluster in Industrials, Technology, and Healthcare • Correlated sector downturns lead to synchronized drawdowns across activist portfolios
Section IV: Limitations & Risk
Asymmetric Payoffs & Outcome Dispersion
Evidence from Prior Research
Litigation
Poison Pills

• Activist returns are highly dispersed: A small number of campaigns generate a disproportionate share of total value, while many deliver modest or negative outcomes • Early alpha is not persistent: Aggressive activists may outperform initially, but return advantages fade postannouncement in multiple studies • Announcement pops are short-lived: Targets can experience ~5% abnormal returns within ~16 trading days, which do not reliably translate into long-term excess returns
Implications for Risk-Adjusted Performance

• Headline IRRs are misleading when volatility, drawdowns, and tail risk are ignored • Activism must be assessed as a portfolio strategy, using: • Sharpe (total volatility) • Sortino (downside risk) • Treynor (market beta exposure)
Section IV: Limitations & Risk
Regulatory & Ecosystem Risks:
Why control and outcomes depend on rules, not just ownership
Ownership Concentration Limits Activist Control
Regulation Shifts Execution Risk & Expected Returns
Litigation

• Activist positions are economically meaningful but structurally non-controlling (~1–10%) • Top 10 holders control ~45% of shares at large-cap U.S. companies; Big Three control ~25% • Outcomes are institution-driven, not ownership-driven
Poison Pills

• Accelerated disclosure (13D / 13G modernization) compresses activists’ stealth window, raising entry prices and reducing optionality • Universal proxy mechanics increase shareholder choice but introduce vote-splitting risk, raising dispersion in contested outcomes • Institutional voters operate under fiduciary and regulatory constraints, expanding the influence of governance norms and proxy advisors over pure return maximization
Ownership ≠ control Control ≠ economic logic
Control = votes × rules
Activist investing is as much about navigating a regulated voting
ecosystem as identifying undervalued assets

Section V: Case Studies
Structural Activism – Case Study
Elliott and AT&T
Involved Parties: Position / Action / Results
• Position: Elliott quietly builds a minority equity stake in AT&T of approximately $3.2b in 2019
• Action: Aggressive public campaign pushing for asset divestments, deleveraging and strategic focus
• Name: Elliott Investment Management • Founder: Paul Singer • Founded: 1977 • Type: Activist hedge fund
• Results: Spin-off of media business through separation of WarnerMedia and DirecTV from AT&T’s core telecom business, reducing conglomerate discount
• Name: AT&T Inc. • Founder: Alexander Graham Bell • Founded: 1885 • Type: Telecommunications company

The campaign of Elliott Management against AT&T is a clear example of structural activism. Elliott built a significant minority stake in stealth and launched a public campaign through a detailed letter criticizing AT&T’s capital allocation and strategy. By maintaining pressure and signaling a credible threat of a proxy fight, Elliott pushed AT&T to engage, leading to strategic simplification, governance changes, and the eventual separation of WarnerMedia and DirecTV from AT&T’s core telecom business. This led to a meaningful share price recovery during the campaign period and generated substantial returns for Elliott.
Section V: Case Studies
Operational Activism – Case Study
Pershing Square and Canadian Pacific Railway
Involved Parties: Position / Action / Results
• Position: Pershing Square builds a significant minority stake of approximately 14% in Canadian Pacific Railway in 2011
• Name: Pershing Square Holdings • Founder: William A. Ackman • Founded: 2004 • Type: Activist hedge fund
• Action: Aggressive campaign, including a proxy fight to replace CEO and board members, supported by detailed competitor benchmarking and an operational turnaround plan
• Results: Replacement of senior management with industry veterans, sharp improvements in operating efficiency and margins, major valuation re-rating
• Name: Canadian Pacific Railway • Founder: George Stephen • Founded: 1881 • Type: Railway transportation company

Pershing Square’s campaign against Canadian Pacific shows how operational activism can unlock value. In 2011, Ackman invested $1.1b for a large minority stake and ran a proxy fight to replace the CEO and the board. The new CEO was rail veteran Hunter Harrison, and some of the new board members were Pershing Square employees. The following operational overhaul achieved substantial improvements in efficiency, profitability, and shareholder value. Pershing Square exited in 2016 with significant profits.
Section V: Case Studies
Governance Activism – Case Study
Engine No.1 and ExxonMobil
Involved Parties: Position / Action / Results
• Name: Engine No. 1 • Founder: Christopher James • Founded: 2020 • Type: Activist hedge fund (“impact driven ownership”)

• Position: Engine No. 1 builds a relatively small Exxon stake (reported ~$40m in Dec 2020) • Action: Launches a proxy contest (Dec 2020) and nominates 4 directors, arguing Exxon needs stronger board oversight, better capital allocation discipline, and credible long-term strategy • Results: Shareholders elect 3 Engine No. 1 nominees to Exxon’s board in 2021. Exxon also states it would reconsider shareholder proposals that won majority support on lobbying/climate reporting
• Name: ExxonMobil Corporation • Founder: N/A (formed via merger of Exxon + Mobil) • Founded: 1999 • Type: Integrated oil & gas major

Engine No. 1's campaign against ExxonMobil challenges the traditional axiom that “might makes right“ in corporate governance, demonstrating that a strategic narrative can outweigh raw capital. With only a 0.02% stake, the fund bypassed the need for a controlling interest by treating passive index giants (BlackRock and Vanguard) as constituents to be won over. By reframing climate inaction as a fundamental failure of capital allocation rather than solely an environmental issue, they successfully mobilized institutional voters to replace three directors.
Section V: Case Studies
Short Activism – Case Study
Hindenburg Research and Nikola Motors
Involved Parties: Position / Action / Results
• Name: Hindenburg Research • Founder: Nate Anderson • Founded: 2017 • Type: Short-Only research firm

• Position: Discloses a short position in Nikola (NKLA) ahead of publication (10 Sep 2020) • Action: Publishes a forensic report alleging systemic misrepresentation (incl. the “Nikola One in Motion” video being staged) • Results: Immediate sell-off; SEC begins examining the allegations 4 days after report publishing; Milton resigns (21 Sep 2020); later Nikola pays $125m to settle SEC charges (Dec 2021) and files Chapter 11 (Feb 2025)
• Name: Nikola Motor Company • Founder: Trevor Milton • Founded: 2014 • Type: Battery-electric + hydrogen fuel-cell truck manufacturer

Hindenburg Research's campaign against Nikola Motors demonstrates how activist hedge funds can assume a regulatory function in global equity markets. It was not the SEC or another official institution that uncovered Nikola's active investor fraud. Rather, it was Hindenburg Research's independent forensic investigation that identified key issues, including a video showing a "rolling" Nikola One truck having been recorded on a downhill road. This video identified the company as grossly overstating its technical developments. The activist report led to an SEC investigation, jail term for Trevor Milton and an eventual delisting of Nikola Motors.
Section V: Case Studies
Poison Pill – Case Study
Icahn and Netflix
Involved Parties: Position / Action / Results
• Position: In 2012, Icahn acquires a meaningful minority stake of approximately $321m (~10%) in Netflix, signaling activist intentions and openly suggesting a sale of the company
• Name: Icahn Enterprises L.P. • Founder: Carl C. Icahn • Founded: 1987 • Type: Activist hedge fund
• Defensive Action: Netflix adopts a poison pill, allowing existent shareholders to buy at a discount to prevent Icahn from increasing his stake beyond a threshold of 10%
• Results: Icahn does not increase his stake but still earns ~$2b on his investment; Netflix remains independent
• Name: Netflix, Inc. • Founder: Reed Hastings, Marc Randolph • Founded: 1997 • Type: Entertainment company

Following his disclosure of a minority stake in Netflix, Icahn quickly escalated by publicly arguing that the company was a logical acquisition target and openly suggesting a sale. This triggered Netflix to adopt a poison pill that stopped Icahn from increasing his stake. Icahn later agreed to a standstill. The stock performed strongly, and Icahn exited with roughly $2b in gains. This case is a strong example of an effective poison pill: it was adopted within days of Icahn’s disclosure, never triggered, acted purely as a deterrent and allowed Netflix to continue performing strongly.
